vocabulary.name: Vocabulary
vocabulary.description: Useful academic and everyday words to grow your vocabulary.

words.meaning: large in amount, size or importance
words.example: The study found a substantial increase in rents.

words.meaning: to make something bad less severe
words.example: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of heat waves.

words.meaning: certain to happen; impossible to avoid
words.example: Some job losses are inevitable as technology changes.
Oil prices fluctuated throughout the year.
Lack of sleep is detrimental to memory.

words.meaning: to publicly support an idea or policy
words.example: Many experts advocate free public transport.

words.meaning: including all or nearly all parts of something
words.example: The report gives a comprehensive overview of the problem.
Constant criticism can undermine a student's confidence.

words.meaning: common or widespread at a particular time
words.example: Online shopping is now prevalent in most cities.
Fuel became expensive; consequently, fewer people drove.

words.meaning: to give a share of something for a particular purpose
words.example: The city allocated more money to public parks.
Air quality deteriorated during the summer.

words.meaning: able to continue without harming the environment or running out
words.example: We need more sustainable sources of energy.

words.meaning: a difference between things that should be the same
words.example: There is a discrepancy between the two sets of figures.

words.meaning: to improve the quality or value of something
words.example: Good lighting can enhance a small room.

words.meaning: belonging to the present time; modern
words.example: The museum focuses on contemporary art.

words.meaning: having more than one possible meaning; unclear
words.example: The question was ambiguous, so answers varied.
Building a bridge here is not financially feasible.
The notion that money brings happiness is debated.

words.meaning: to make it difficult for something to happen
words.example: Poor internet access can hinder online learning.

phrasal.name: Phrasal Verbs
phrasal.description: Common phrasal verbs used in everyday conversation.

words.example: I can't figure out how this works.
Don't give up - you're almost there.

words.meaning: to find or meet by chance
words.example: I came across an old photo yesterday.
We put off the trip until spring.

words.meaning: to feel happy about something that will happen
words.example: I look forward to hearing from you.

words.meaning: to use all of something so none is left
words.example: We ran out of milk.

words.meaning: to start talking about a subject
words.example: She brought up an interesting point.
Carry on - I'm listening.

words.meaning: to refuse an offer or request
words.example: He turned down the job offer.

words.meaning: to reach the same level as others, or to talk after time apart
words.example: Let's catch up over coffee.
She pointed out a mistake in my code.
Can you set up the meeting room?
I get along well with my roommate.

words.meaning: to exercise, or to find a solution
words.example: Things will work out in the end.
I'll look into the problem today.

words.meaning: to arrive, often unexpectedly or late
words.example: He showed up an hour late.
The game was called off because of rain.

words.meaning: to handle a problem or situation
words.example: I'll deal with the emails later.

words.meaning: to finally be in a place or situation you didn't plan
words.example: We ended up staying until midnight.

words.meaning: to review or check something carefully
words.example: Let's go over the plan once more.

idioms.name: Idioms
idioms.description: Idioms native speakers use all the time.

words.meaning: to make people feel more relaxed when they first meet
words.example: He told a joke to break the ice.
I'm a bit under the weather today.
I need to hit the books before the exam.
The test was a piece of cake.

words.meaning: agreeing or understanding something in the same way
words.example: Let's make sure we're on the same page.

words.meaning: to stop working for the day
words.example: It's late - let's call it a day.

words.text: cost an arm and a leg
words.example: That phone cost an arm and a leg.

words.meaning: to learn how to do something
words.example: You'll get the hang of it soon.

words.text: the ball is in your court
words.meaning: it is your turn to decide or act
words.example: I've made my offer; the ball is in your court.
I eat fast food once in a blue moon.
Stop beating around the bush and tell me.

words.meaning: to do something cheaply or quickly by skipping steps
words.example: Don't cut corners on safety.
He's in hot water for missing the deadline.
Can you keep an eye on my bag?

words.meaning: to lose an opportunity by being too slow
words.example: Tickets sold out - we missed the boat.

words.meaning: to joke with someone by telling them something untrue
words.example: Relax, I'm just pulling your leg.
You can't sit on the fence forever.

words.meaning: the final problem that makes a situation unacceptable
words.example: Being late again was the last straw.
We need to think outside the box here.
Who spilled the beans about the party?

casual.name: Casual
casual.description: Everyday spoken English you'll hear from friends and coworkers.

words.meaning: to spend time relaxing with someone
words.example: Want to hang out after work?

words.meaning: it's fine; don't worry about it
words.example: "Sorry I'm late!" "No worries."
My bad, I sent you the wrong file.

words.meaning: I'd like to join; I agree to the plan
words.example: Pizza tonight? I'm down.

words.meaning: to get something quick to eat
words.example: Let's grab a bite before the movie.
I have to go - catch you later!

words.meaning: I agree; that plan works for me
words.example: "Meet at six?" "Sounds good."
You forgot? It's no big deal.
Just a heads-up: the meeting moved to 3 pm.
Long day - I'm beat.
Put your wallet away, it's on me.

words.meaning: contact me; send me a message
words.example: Hit me up if you need help.

words.meaning: seriously; truly (also asks if something is true)
words.example: You got the job? For real?
I'm kind of hungry.
The concert was cancelled - what a bummer.

words.meaning: relaxed and calm; or to relax
words.example: Let's just chill at home tonight.

words.meaning: a casual hello; what is happening?
words.example: Hey, what's up?
Oh, now I get it!
I gotta go, my bus is here.
Take it easy this weekend!

motivation.name: Motivation
motivation.description: Short lines to keep you going.

words.text: Small steps every day add up to big results.
words.meaning: Progress comes from consistency, not from one big effort.
Finishing something imperfect beats never finishing.

words.text: You don't have to feel ready to start.
words.meaning: Confidence often comes after you begin, not before.

words.text: Discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want now.
Every expert was once a beginner.
words.meaning: Being bad at something new is normal.

words.text: Rest is part of the work.
One page, one word, one rep at a time.
words.meaning: Break big goals into tiny actions.

words.text: Mistakes are proof that you are trying.
words.meaning: Errors mean you're learning, not failing.

words.text: Focus on the next right step.
words.meaning: You don't need the whole plan to move forward.

words.text: Comparison steals joy - compete with who you were yesterday.
words.meaning: Measure progress against your past self.

words.text: Start where you are, use what you have.
A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
words.meaning: Proverb (Chinese, from the Tao Te Ching): every big achievement starts small.

words.text: Fall seven times, stand up eight.
words.meaning: Japanese proverb: resilience matters more than falling.
Moving forward at any speed counts.

math.description: Key formulas from algebra, geometry, trigonometry and physics.

Area of a circle with radius r.

words.text: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°
words.meaning: The three interior angles of any triangle sum to 180 degrees.
The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.

Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: energy equals mass times the speed of light squared.
Euler's identity, linking five fundamental constants.

poems.name: Poems
poems.description: Famous lines from classic poems (all in the public domain).

words.text:
Hope is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
And sings the tune without the words,
And never stops at all.
words.meaning: Emily Dickinson - "Hope is the thing with feathers" (1891). Hope as a small bird that never stops singing.

words.text:
Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—
I took the one less traveled by,
And that has made all the difference.
words.meaning: Robert Frost - "The Road Not Taken" (1916). About choices and their lasting effect.

words.text:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate.

To see a World in a Grain of Sand
And a Heaven in a Wild Flower,
Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand
And Eternity in an hour.
words.meaning: William Blake - "Auguries of Innocence" (1863). Finding the whole universe in small things.

words.text:
I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils.
words.meaning: William Wordsworth - "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud" (1807).

words.text:
A thing of beauty is a joy for ever:
Its loveliness increases; it will never
Pass into nothingness.
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
words.meaning: Alfred, Lord Tennyson - "Ulysses" (1842). Never giving up.

words.text:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
words.meaning: Percy Bysshe Shelley - "Ozymandias" (1818). Even great power fades.

words.text:
I am the master of my fate,
I am the captain of my soul.
words.meaning: William Ernest Henley - "Invictus" (1888). Inner strength in hard times.

words.text:
If you can keep your head when all about you
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you…
words.meaning: Rudyard Kipling - "If—" (1910). Staying calm under pressure.

words.text:
I'm Nobody! Who are you?
Are you – Nobody – too?
words.meaning: Emily Dickinson - "I'm Nobody! Who are you?" (1891).

words.text:
O my Luve is like a red, red rose
That's newly sprung in June.

She walks in beauty, like the night
Of cloudless climes and starry skies.

Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land.
